nodes.label: The archive as object
nodes.date_label: Le goût de l'archive 1989 · Archive Fever 1994/1996 · Silencing the Past 1995 · Dust 2001 · Archival Science 2 'archives, records, and power' 2002 · Archive Stories 2005 · 'Venus in Two Acts' 2008 · Along the Archival Grain 2009 · Dispossessed Lives 2016 · Trouillot Remixed 2021
nodes.description: This editorial grouping brings together distinct inquiries into archives as institutions, practices, sources and objects of interpretation. Trouillot's Silencing the Past (1995) located the silences of history in 'the making of sources', 'the making of archives', 'the making of narratives' and 'the making of history in the final instance' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020), and made the Haitian Revolution the case of an event 'unthinkable' as it happened. Stoler asked colonial historians to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (2002) and to read 'along the archival grain' before reading against it, finding in Dutch colonial records a 'repository of good taste and bad faith' (2009, as quoted by Gouda). Farge's Le goût de l'archive (1989), Derrida's Archive Fever (1994) and Steedman's Dust (2001) wrote the archive's allure, fever and dust; Schwartz and Cook, from the archival profession, called archives 'active sites where social power is negotiated' (2002); Burton's Archive Stories (2005) collected historians' encounters with their sources; Hartman's 'critical fabulation' (2008) and Fuentes (2016) confronted the violence of slavery's archive.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier works: Arlette Farge, Le goût de l'archive (1989; The Allure of the Archives, 2013, foreword Natalie Zemon Davis); Thomas Richards, The Imperial Archive (1993); Jacques Derrida, Mal d'archive / Archive Fever (lecture 1994; Diacritics 1995; Chicago 1996); Michel-Rolph Trouillot, Silencing the Past (1995; 20th-anniversary edition with Hazel V. Carby's foreword, 2015); Saidiya Hartman, Scenes of Subjection (1997). Selected interventions: the History of the Human Sciences issue 'The Archive' (1999); Terry Cook, 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth' (Archivaria 51, 2001); Carolyn Steedman, Dust and 'Something She Called a Fever' (2001); Archival Science 2:1–2, 'archives, records, and power' (2002: Joan M. Schwartz and Terry Cook; Ann Laura Stoler, 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance'); Refiguring the Archive (2002: Achille Mbembe, 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits'; Stoler); From the Margins (2002: Nicholas B. Dirks, 'Annals of the Archive'); Diana Taylor, The Archive and the Repertoire (2003); Ann Cvetkovich, An Archive of Feelings (2003); Marlene Manoff, 'Theories of the Archive from Across the Disciplines' (2004); Antoinette Burton, ed., Archive Stories (2005: Durba Ghosh, Tony Ballantyne, Adele Perry, Ann Curthoys). Later contributions: Stoler, Along the Archival Grain (2009) and the Bijdragen debate (Gouda, Raben, Schulte Nordholt, 2009); Anjali Arondekar, For the Record (2009); Hartman, 'Venus in Two Acts' (Small Axe 26, 2008); Francis X. Blouin and William G. Rosenberg, Processing the Past (2011); David Zeitlyn, 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (2012); Marisa J. Fuentes, Dispossessed Lives (2016); Trouillot Remixed (2021). Readers: Frances Gouda, Remco Raben, Henk Schulte Nordholt (2009); Alyssa Goldstein Sepinwall (2013); Marlene L. Daut (2021); Bastien Craipain (2024).
nodes.scope_note: A Research-field entry gathering a readership rather than a school: in the History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) the share of Canada + US theses citing two or more of Stoler, Trouillot, Farge, Derrida, Hartman, Steedman, Burton, Fuentes, Blouin and Rosenberg rose from 0 (1990s) to 3.3% (2000–09), 7.1%, 7.6% and 10.4% (2020–25; US 11.8%, Canada 9.0%; Europe 2.1%), with Stoler cited by 10.7% of theses in 2020–25 across 11 of 18 fields and Trouillot by 5.9%; no opposing side is co-cited (cohorts README §5), and Along the Archival Grain entered the global/transnational neighbourhood of PhDs in 2020–25. Six strands: the archive as a site of power (Trouillot, Mbembe, Schwartz and Cook); reading along the grain (Stoler); allure, fever and dust (Farge, Derrida, Steedman); absence, violence and critical fabulation (Hartman, Fuentes); archive stories and the ethnography of archives (Burton, Dirks, Zeitlyn); the archivists' turn in Canada and South Africa (Cook, Schwartz, Harris, Brothman). Research of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md): read in full — Gouda (2009), Schulte Nordholt (2009), Ottevaere (2004), Schultz (2015), Craipain (2024), the Chicago obituary and the finding aid for Trouillot; in part — Cook (2001), the Bulamah–Goyatá–Pereira introduction (2020), Davidson (2020); abstracts and contents only — Stoler 2002, Schwartz and Cook 2002, Mbembe 2002, Manoff 2004, Trouillot 2003, Along the Archival Grain, Archive Stories, From the Margins, Haunted by Empire, Duress, For the Record, The Archive and the Repertoire. Unread: the bodies of Silencing the Past (the four-moments passage is given as later writers list it and as Davidson quotes it, unpaginated; wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of ch. 1), Along the Archival Grain, Carnal Knowledge, Archive Fever, Dust and the AHR essay, Le goût de l'archive, 'Venus in Two Acts', Dispossessed Lives, The Imperial Archive, Processing the Past, Zeitlyn 2012, the HHS 1999 issue, Sepinwall 2013, Daut 2021, Carby's foreword. Richards (1993), Blouin and Rosenberg (2011) and the HHS issue are named in the works list but not dated as events (no page reached). Indigenous data sovereignty and the digital archive are out of scope (see web_history for the 2024 uptake of Stoler's phrase).

strands.title: The archive as a site of power: Trouillot, Mbembe, Schwartz and Cook
strands.focus: Trouillot's Silencing the Past (1995) holds that silences enter historical production at four moments — 'fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020) — and that 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020, unpaginated; wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of ch. 1). Craipain (2024) reads the book as a 'critical indictment of Western historiography' whose 'historical guild' relegated 'racism, slavery and colonialism' to 'an historical backburner' (Trouillot, p. 98, as quoted by Craipain). From the archival profession, Schwartz and Cook opened Archival Science's 'archives, records, and power' issues (2002) with the claim that archives 'are not passive storehouses of old stuff, but active sites where social power is negotiated' (abstract); Mbembe's 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits' (2002) begins from the archive as 'a building, a symbol of a public institution' (abstract).
strands.works: Silencing the Past (1995); 'The Power of the Archive and its Limits' (2002); 'Archives, Records, and Power' (2002)

strands.title: Reading along the grain: Stoler's ethnography of the colonial archive
strands.focus: Stoler's 2002 essay asked anthropologists in colonial studies, whose 'archival activity tends to remain more an extractive than an ethnographic one', to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (abstract). Along the Archival Grain (2009) treated Dutch colonial records 'not just as repositories of state power, but as unquiet movements in a field of force' (pp. 32–33, as quoted by Schulte Nordholt), looked 'for the pulse of the archive in the quiescence and quickened pace of its own production' (p. 35) and aimed 'to set a new standard for an ethnography of the archives' (p. 45) rather than an ethnography in them. Gouda: she 'underscores the necessity to read along the grain before trying to read against it, as many postcolonial scholars in recent years have advocated' (2009, p. 552). The reviewers' doubts are part of the record: Schulte Nordholt was 'not quite sure how to identify these "pulses"' and found 'an unexpected colonial flavour' in a book that ignored archives in Indonesia and Indonesian scholars (pp. 560, 562); Gouda found 'so little engagement with the work of contemporary Dutch historians' (p. 555).
strands.works: 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002); Along the Archival Grain (2009); the Bijdragen debate (2009)

strands.title: Allure, fever and dust: Farge, Derrida, Steedman
strands.focus: Three texts made the historian's experience of the archive their subject. Farge's Le goût de l'archive (1989; English 2013, with Natalie Zemon Davis's foreword) is, in Yale's words, a reflection on the sensory and emotional experience of archival work in the judicial records of eighteenth-century Paris; Arnold Hunt called it 'an eloquent testimony to the materiality of the archive and its power to astonish and delight'. Derrida's Archive Fever (lecture 1994; Diacritics 1995; Chicago 1996), already on the derrida, memory and freud entries, is 'an extended meditation on remembrance, religion, time, and technology' that starts from archiving (publisher). Steedman's Dust (2001) and 'Something She Called a Fever: Michelet, Derrida, and Dust' (AHR 106:4, 2001) answered Derrida with the archive as the repository of 'that which will not go away' and named 'archivization' as the practice of attending to it (publisher description). Terry Cook dated the 'Derrida aftershock', in which historians and others were 'subjecting the archival world to a detailed critique such as it has never before experienced', from inside the profession (2001, p. 21). All three bodies unread.
strands.works: Le goût de l'archive (1989); Archive Fever (1994/1996); Dust (2001); 'Something She Called a Fever' (2001)

strands.title: Absence, violence and critical fabulation: Hartman, Fuentes
strands.focus: Hartman's 'Venus in Two Acts' (Small Axe 26, June 2008) examines a girl's presence and silence in the archive of Atlantic slavery; the MacArthur Foundation describes her 'speculative method she terms "critical fabulation," which questions historical archives as the sole source of credible information about the past' (2019). Scenes of Subjection (1997) 'traces continuities between pre- and post-emancipation eras' (MacArthur). Fuentes's Dispossessed Lives (2016), on enslaved and free women in eighteenth-century Bridgetown, 'interrogates the archive and its historical production to expose the ongoing effects' of slavery's violence, 'combining fragmentary sources with interdisciplinary methodologies that include black feminist theory' (publisher). Both are unread here; the strand records their place in the readership (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: Hartman 4.3% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, from 0 in 2000–09; Fuentes a 2020–25 entrant to the US capitalism and Indigenous networks).
strands.works: Scenes of Subjection (1997); 'Venus in Two Acts' (2008); Dispossessed Lives (2016)

strands.title: Archive stories and the ethnography of archives: Burton, Dirks, Zeitlyn
strands.focus: Burton's Archive Stories (Duke, 2005) collected, in the press's words, ethnographies of the archival world by historians that challenge 'the claims to objectivity associated with the traditional archive'; its introduction is titled 'Archive Fever, Archive Stories', and its contributors include Durba Ghosh on miscegenation in Britain and India, Tony Ballantyne on 'Mr. Peal's Archive', Jennifer Milligan on 'What Is an Archive?' in modern France, Adele Perry on 'The Colonial Archive on Trial' in Delgamuukw v. British Columbia, and Ann Curthoys. Dirks's 'Annals of the Archive: Ethnographic Notes on the Sources of History' opened Part 1, 'Ethnography and the Archive', of From the Margins (2002), the volume that also printed Stoler and Trouillot. Zeitlyn's 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (Annual Review of Anthropology 41, 2012) and Manoff's survey of 'theories of the archive from across the disciplines' (2004), which found 'a confluence of interests among scholars, archivists, and librarians', mark the turn's consolidation. All bodies unread; the strand rests on contents and abstracts.
strands.works: From the Margins (2002); The Archive and the Repertoire (2003); 'Theories of the Archive from Across the Disciplines' (2004); Archive Stories (2005); 'Anthropology in and of the Archives' (2012)

strands.title: The archivists' turn: Canada and South Africa
strands.focus: The profession's own turn ran beside and partly before the historians'. Cook names 'the pioneering postmodern archivists before Cook' as 'also Canadian, Brien Brothman and Richard Brown' (2001, n. 13). His plenary to the Association of Canadian Archivists (Winnipeg, 8 June 2001), printed as 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth', argued that appraisal should let archives 'acquire in its holdings multiple voices, and not by default only the voices of the powerful', while, 'as Verne Harris notes', not romanticising the marginalised (pp. 31–32), and that 'the Canadian parallel way of archival remembering through macro-appraisal may speak strongly to archivists in this new century' (p. 32). Schwartz (National Archives of Canada / Queen's) and Cook (Manitoba) then edited the 'archives, records, and power' issues of Archival Science (2002), citing Derrida and Harris, not Foucault or Stoler (reference list). Harris's South African work and Refiguring the Archive (2002) are the other pole. Perry's chapter on the colonial archive before the courts in Delgamuukw (2005) is the Canadian historians' link, unread.
strands.works: 'What Is Past Is Prologue' (1997); 'Fashionable Nonsense or Professional Rebirth' (2001); 'Archives, Records, and Power' (2002); Refiguring the Archive (2002)

nodes.label: Ann Laura Stoler
nodes.date_label: 'Tensions of Empire' (with Cooper) 1989 · Race and the Education of Desire 1995 · Tensions of Empire 1997 · 'Tense and Tender Ties' 2001 · 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' 2002 · Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power 2002 · Haunted by Empire 2006 · Along the Archival Grain 2009 · Imperial Debris 2013 · Duress 2016
nodes.description: An American anthropologist of Dutch and French colonial rule who moved from Sumatra's plantation belt to the colonial archive itself. With Frederick Cooper she set an agenda for reading metropole and colony together (1989; 1997). Race and the Education of Desire (1995) questioned race and empire in Foucault's history of sexuality; Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002) asked why 'Foucault's elusive and suggestive treatment of race still remains so marginal to what colonial historians take from him' (p. 141) and treated 'colonizer/colonized' as 'a historically shifting pair of social categories that needs to be explained' (p. 13; both as quoted by Ottevaere, 2004). 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002) asked scholars to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject'; Along the Archival Grain (2009) read Dutch records 'along the grain' for 'the pulse of the archive' (p. 35, as quoted by Schulte Nordholt) and 'the habits of the colonial heart' (p. 53, as quoted by Gouda). Imperial Debris (2013) and Duress (2016) turned to ruination and 'imperial durabilities'. Gouda: in postcolonial studies 'paying homage to Ann Stoler's work has become de rigueur' (2009).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ann Laura Stoler (b. 1949); Capitalism and Confrontation in Sumatra's Plantation Belt, 1870–1979 (1985); with Frederick Cooper, 'Tensions of Empire' (American Ethnologist, 1989) and Tensions of Empire (eds, 1997); Race and the Education of Desire (1995); 'Tense and Tender Ties' (JAH, 2001); 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (Archival Science, 2002); Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002; 2nd ed. 2010); ed., Haunted by Empire (2006); with McGranahan and Perdue, eds, Imperial Formations (2007); Along the Archival Grain (2009); ed., Imperial Debris (2013); Duress (2016); Interior Frontiers (2022). Readers: Dawn Ottevaere (2004); Frances Gouda, Remco Raben, Henk Schulte Nordholt (2009); Ronald Schultz (2015).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md §§1–2, 6): the abstract and reference list of the 2002 Archival Science essay; the contents of Along the Archival Grain and three reviews from the Bijdragen debate (Gouda and Schulte Nordholt in full, Raben's first page) with the first paragraph of Stoler's reply; Ottevaere's H-Net review of Carnal Knowledge (in full) and the UC Press contents; Schultz's H-Net review of Imperial Debris (in full); the Duke pages for Haunted by Empire and Duress. Unread: every book's body, the 2002 essay's body, 'Tense and Tender Ties' (2001), the Cooper–Stoler introductions of 1989 and 1997 (metadata and contents only, as the graph already records), Imperial Formations (2007), Interior Frontiers (2022), and Stoler's reply to her Dutch critics beyond its opening. Her 2002 notes cite Trouillot's Silencing the Past three times; no sentence of hers on Trouillot was read. Quotations from the 2009 book are 'as quoted by' Gouda or Schulte Nordholt, from Carnal Knowledge 'as quoted by' Ottevaere, from Imperial Debris 'as quoted by' Schultz, with their page numbers. Wikidata Q16203101 checked by QLever on 2026-10-23 (born 1949; anthropologist, historian; VIAF 263247736). Posts from the New School's pages (search rendering; the page itself returned 429) and the UC Press author line; the Wisconsin years (1983–89) and degrees (Barnard BA 1972, Columbia PhD 1982) from Wikipedia's citation of New School pages, orientation only; the 1985 book is not dated as an event because no publisher page was fetched. nodes.label: Michel-Rolph Trouillot
nodes.date_label: Ti dife boule sou istwa Ayiti 1977 · Peasants and Capital 1988 · Haiti: State against Nation 1990 · 'The Odd and the Ordinary' 1990 · Silencing the Past 1995 · Global Transformations 2003 · Trouillot Remixed 2021
nodes.description: A Haitian anthropologist and historian who left Port-au-Prince for New York in 1968 and wrote his first history of the Haitian Revolution in Creole (Ti dife boule, 1977). Peasants and Capital (1988) and Haiti: State against Nation (1990) studied Dominica's economy and Duvalierism; 'The Odd and the Ordinary' (1990) refused Haitian exceptionalism. Silencing the Past (1995) asked how power enters 'the production of history': silences enter at four moments, 'fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance'; 'in history, power begins at the source' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020); the Haitian Revolution was 'unthinkable' as it happened, and the 'historical guild' relegated 'racism, slavery and colonialism' to 'an historical backburner' (p. 98, as quoted by Craipain). 'Anthropology and the Savage Slot' and Global Transformations (2003) turned the same question on anthropology's 'North Atlantic universals'. Craipain: Silencing the Past 'remains an unavoidable reference' (2024); Daut asked readers to go 'beyond Trouillot' (2021). Trouillot Remixed (2021) collects the essays.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Michel-Rolph Trouillot (1949–2012); Ti dife boule sou istwa Ayiti (1977; Stirring the Pot of Haitian History, 2021); Peasants and Capital: Dominica in the World Economy (1988); Haiti: State against Nation: The Origins and Legacy of Duvalierism (1990); 'The Odd and the Ordinary: Haiti, the Caribbean, and the World' (Cimarrón, 1990); Silencing the Past: Power and the Production of History (1995; 20th-anniversary edition 2015, foreword Hazel V. Carby); Open the Social Sciences (Gulbenkian Commission, 1996); 'Abortive Rituals: Historical Apologies in the Global Era' (2000); 'Culture on the Edges' (2002); Global Transformations: Anthropology and the Modern World (2003), including 'Anthropology and the Savage Slot' (first printing reported as 1991, not verified) and 'The Anthropology of the State in the Age of Globalization'; Trouillot Remixed (2021). Readers: Alyssa Goldstein Sepinwall (2013); Colin Dayan, J. Michael Dash, Greg Beckett (2013); Hazel V. Carby (2015); Rodrigo Bulamah, Júlia Goyatá and Bethânia Pereira (2020); Marlene L. Daut (2021); Yarimar Bonilla (2021); Bastien Craipain (2024).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md §§4, 13): the University of Chicago obituary (2012) and the Chicago Library finding aid's biographical note (in full); the contents and descriptions of Silencing the Past (Beacon), Global Transformations (Springer, with the 'Savage Slot' abstract) and Trouillot Remixed (Duke); the Journal of Haitian Studies 19:2 (2013) contents; Craipain's H-Net review of Stirring the Pot (2024, in full); the Bulamah–Goyatá–Pereira introduction to 'The Odd and the Ordinary' (Vibrant, 2020, in part); Davidson's Overland essay (2020), which quotes chapter 1 without page numbers. Unread: every book's body — the four-moments passage of Silencing the Past is given as later writers list it and as Davidson quotes it, unpaginated, and its wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1; chapter 3, 'An Unthinkable History', by title and Craipain's quotation (p. 98) only; Haiti: State against Nation and Peasants and Capital by obituary citations only; Sepinwall (2013), Daut (2021), Carby (2015), Bonilla's prelude (2021) and Dayan (2012–13) are named as readers but unread. The first printing of 'Anthropology and the Savage Slot' (reported as 1991), the Current Anthropology date of the state essay (reported as 2001) and the dates of the Johns Hopkins chair and Institute are not verified by a page read and are not asserted. Wikidata Q6836249 checked by QLever on 2026-10-23. Born 26 November 1949, Port-au-Prince (Wikidata); son and nephew of the historians Ernest and Hénock Trouillot (Bulamah et al., n. 3); Duke 1983–88, Johns Hopkins 1988–98, Chicago 1998–2012 (finding aid); died 5 July 2012 aged 62 after an aneurysm (obituaries). History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23): cited by 5.9% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25 (0.8% in 2000–09), Silencing the Past by 4.3% in 2015–25, in 5 of 18 fields; a figure for this note, not for arrows.

edges.relationship: The archive of Atlantic slavery as the field's hardest case: Hartman's 'Venus in Two Acts' (2008) and the 'critical fabulation' the MacArthur Foundation describes (2019); Fuentes's Dispossessed Lives (2016), which 'interrogates the archive and its historical production' for Bridgetown's enslaved and free women (publisher)

edges.relationship: An editorial comparison: Cook presented the archival profession's engagement as 'postmodernism and the practice of archives' (2001) and Manoff found 'a confluence of interests among scholars, archivists, and librarians' begun by Derrida and Foucault (2004), while Stoler's programme reads 'along the grain' before reading against it (as Gouda puts it, 2009)
edges.evidence_note: Cook 2001 title and abstract (read); Manoff's abstract (DSpace record); Gouda 2009, p. 552 (read). An editorial comparison placed by the atlas, not a succession claimed by any text read; no text read names the linguistic turn as its target (reworded after review, finding 8).

edges.relationship: Asked colonial studies to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' and from 'extractive' to 'ethnographic' archival work (2002); read the Dutch colonial archive 'along the grain' for 'the pulse of the archive' and set out 'to set a new standard for an ethnography of the archives' (2009, pp. 35, 45, as quoted by Schulte Nordholt)

edges.relationship: With Cooper, an agenda for reading metropole and colony together (1989; 1997); Carnal Knowledge argued that 'students of colonialism, anthropologists in particular, have taken the politically constructed dichotomy colonizer/colonized as a given rather than as a historically shifting pair of social categories' (2002, p. 13, as quoted by Ottevaere, 2004); Gouda: homage to her work 'has become de rigueur' in postcolonial studies
edges.evidence_note: Ottevaere 2004 (read in full), quoting pp. 9, 13 and 15; Gouda 2009, pp. 553–554 (read); Crossref for the 1989 introduction; the graph's existing record of Tensions of Empire (contents). The 1989 and 1997 introductions are unread. The post entry's strands colonial_intimacies and metropole_colony already name her.

edges.relationship: Silencing the Past (1995) placed the archive inside the production of history: silences enter at 'the moment of fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)'; 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' (all as quoted by Davidson, 2020); Stoler's 2002 essay cites it three times

Body unread; corrected after review (finding 13). Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).

edges.relationship: Ti dife boule sou istwa Ayiti (Brooklyn, 1977), a Creole history of the revolution written in exile by a group that 'harbored an anti- or rather a counter-academism … to oppose the knowledge embargo imposed by the "official" venues of knowledge production' (Lyonel Trouillot, as quoted by Craipain); 'virtually absent from bibliographies in North Atlantic academia' until the 2021 translation

edges.relationship: Silencing the Past 'remains an unavoidable reference for anyone navigating the streams of Black and Caribbean studies in academia and beyond' (Craipain, 2024); Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira read 'The Odd and the Ordinary' as challenging an exceptionalist image that isolates Haiti from its surrounding world (2020, paragraph 5)

edges.relationship: 'A critical indictment of Western historiography and its systematic disregard for Haiti's contribution to emancipatory struggles and decolonial politics', offering 'an eye-opening analysis of the epistemological failures and ideological maneuverings intrinsic to history telling as a professional activity' (Craipain, 2024); 'As Trouillot taught us, not all narratives or narrators are created equal'

edges.relationship: 'The Presence in the Past' (1995, ch. 5), 'Good Day, Columbus: Silences, Power, and Public History (1492–1892)' and 'Abortive Rituals: Historical Apologies in the Global Era' (2000) took commemoration and apology as moments of 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020); in Davidson's exposition, silences are produced and reproduced throughout any telling of a story
edges.evidence_note: Chapter and essay titles (Beacon and Duke contents, read); Davidson 2020 (read), whose block quotation gives the fourth moment in Trouillot's words; the sentence 'Silences are produced and reproduced throughout any telling of a story' is Davidson's own exposition, not a Trouillot quotation (corrected after review, finding 13). Thin: no body read. Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).

edges.relationship: A settler-colonial analytic worked out in conversation with Native American and Indigenous Studies: US Indian policy (removal, allotment, blood quantum, termination) read as successive modalities of elimination (2006, 2011); 'a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking' (Goeman, 2016)
edges.evidence_note: Goeman 2016 (read in full): "a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking and scholarship that exists far longer than settler nations"; "He critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner". Kauanui 2016 (read in full), note 7: "his long time, direct intellectual engagement with scholars in Native American and Indigenous Studies", and para. 2: he insisted "that Native scholars did" create the field. Wolfe 2006 (read in full), sections on discovery and preemption, the Cherokee removal, allotment, blood quantum ("statistical extermination", quoting Jaimes) and termination; "After the Frontier" (2011) is unread. A contribution to the conversation, not an origin: the entry's Indigenous methods are not derived from him, and the dissent of Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014) is recorded on the entry. Replaces the former comparison row. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Race as the outcome of 'differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process' (2001): 'a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting'; Black people 'racialized as slaves', Indians eliminated 'as Indians' (2006); a comparative typology of colonial race regimes in Traces of History (2016)
edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), opening section: "different racial regimes encode and reproduce the unequal relationships into which Europeans coerced the populations concerned"; "Black people's enslavement produced an inclusive taxonomy … For Indians, in stark contrast, non-Indian ancestry compromised their indigeneity"; "a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; and note 62 quoting his own 2001 essay, p. 894: "Difference … is not simply given. It is the outcome of differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process." The 2001 essay is otherwise unread (Crossref: AHR 106:3, June 2001). Traces of History (2016) known through the British Library contents note (chapters on Australia, the United States, central Europe, Brazil, Palestine) and Veracini's obituary (read): it "utilises his analysis of racism under settler colonialism in order to explain racism everywhere else" and provides "a compelling typology of racial formations". Strengthens the entry-level comparison edge_885, which stays. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Settler colonialism set beside genocide studies: the Holocaust as 'the non-paradigmatic paradigm' against which 'qualified genocides' are devalued; 'structural genocide' proposed to retain settler colonialism's specificity without 'hierarchy among victims'; a chapter in Moses's Empire, Colony, Genocide (2006–08)
edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal"; "The best known of all genocides was internal to Europe"; Lemkin's definition (note 6); Hull, Pohl, Zimmerer and "the modernity of colonialism"; "the Holocaust, the non-paradigmatic paradigm that, being the indispensable example, can never merely exemplify"; "the term 'structural genocide' avoids the questions of degree—and, therefore, of hierarchy among victims" (p. 403 per Kauanui). The 2008 chapter in Moses ed. is unread (Berghahn contents; Docker's "Are Settler-Colonies Inherently Genocidal?" in the same volume). The holocaust entry is historiographical; this compares frames and does not claim he wrote Holocaust history. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Settler against franchise colonialism: settler colonies 'were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour' but 'premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land' (1999), 'a specific social formation' whose specificity is to be retained (2006)
edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 1999, pp. 1–2 (existing reading, cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro: the introduction distinguishes settler from franchise colonies) and p. 3 as quoted by Englert 2020 (read): "In contrast to the kind of colonial formation that Cabral or Fanon confronted settler colonies were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour. Rather, they are premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land". Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "settler colonialism is a specific social formation and it is desirable to retain that specificity". Englert finds the Fanon/Algeria example contradictory (Algeria depended on Indigenous labour). A comparison, not a critique: Hoxie 2008 (existing abstract) places the frame inside postcolonial critique, while Veracini's claim that postcolonial studies missed the settler situation is drawn at entry level (edge_882 revised). (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Treaties, preemption, removal and allotment read as 'the logic of elimination' rather than as relations and encounter: 'the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute [the colonial state's] principal means of expansion' (2006); set against the fur-trade historiography's 'middle ground', which Veracini records as a rival recovery (2013)
edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), second section (the doctrine of discovery, preemption, the Cherokee removal: "The American right to buy always superseded the Indian right not to sell" (Rosenthal, quoted); "Rather than something separate from or running counter to the colonial state, the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute its principal means of expansion") and sixth section (allotment, blood quantum, termination). Veracini 2013, concluding section (author manuscript, read): "the recovery of a long lasting 'middle ground' between indigenous and settler polities in the past, sustained the possibility of renewed relationships"; "both the Canadian and US historiographies were late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis". edge_869 already compares the two fields; this names the person's own reading. Canadian material is not his. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Wolfe took from Harris the sentence that 'the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus' when capital's interest in uncluttered access to land is combined with settlers' interest in land as livelihood (2004, quoted 2006): a use as evidence, moderate
edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), third section and note 36, quoting Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess?" (2004), p. 179: "Combine capital's interest in uncluttered access to land and settlers' interest in land as livelihood, and the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus." Englert 2020 (read) also uses Harris 2004, p. 172, against Wolfe. The direction matters for edge_1014, which found no derivation of Harris from Wolfe: the citation runs the other way. A single quotation; influence in the sense of a use as evidence, as for locB_rel_26 in revision 1.152. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Critiques address both Wolfe's model and its subsequent uses: Macoun and Strakosch question structural inevitability; Rowse questions a teleology of elimination; Englert directly challenges elimination as the defining logic. Kauanui defends Wolfe against formulaic citation while rejecting the replacement of Indigenous Studies (2013–20)
edges.evidence_note: Macoun and Strakosch 2013 (author version, read): "SCT can depict colonization as structurally inevitable"; "Foundational scholar Patrick Wolfe has been labelled 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world'"; "a kind of colonial fatalism"; "it does not account for Indigenous lives". Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014 (read): "treating settler colonialism as a meta-structure, thus erasing both its contingency and the dynamics that co-constitute" it. Rowse 2014 (abstract, existing): a "teleology of elimination". Kauanui 2016 (read in full): a criticism of Wolfe's reception rather than of Wolfe, defending the theory against the phrase that 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement' with it, and asking that "Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies". 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' is the citation graph's category for a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position (Sol review 1.156, finding 3). Englert 2020 (read in full): "a critique of the Wolfe-an model"; elimination "does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism, as claimed by Wolfe". Fairness: Kauanui and Goeman record his disclaimers and his engagement with NAIS; Macoun and Strakosch call his contribution "vital". (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Settler colonialism against underdevelopment: the 1970s–80s 'settler/dominion capitalism' literature made the settler colony 'the opposite of colonialism and associated underdevelopment' (Veracini 2013 on Denoon 1983); Englert returns the question through Harvey's accumulation by dispossession (2020)
edges.evidence_note: Veracini 2013 (abstract, existing record; author manuscript read): in the third phase "settler colonialism is understood as the opposite of colonialism and associated underdevelopment and political fragmentation", and the settler-capitalism approach wrote "indigenous people and indigenous history off the conceptual map". Denoon 1983 at title level (existing). Englert 2020 (read in full): accumulation by dispossession "as developed by David Harvey (2003)" proposed as the alternative to the elimination model, with Emmanuel's 1972 NLR essay on white-settler colonialism in his bibliography. A comparison of frames; no descent asserted. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: The settler order as a frame for Canadian working-class history (Burrill 2019); settler workers as participants in 'accumulation by dispossession' who 'fight simultaneously over the distribution of wealth generated through their labour and the distribution of the colonial loot' (Englert 2020)
edges.evidence_note: Burrill 2019 (abstract, existing record screq_burrill_2019; the strand cdn_working_class/indigenous_labour_settler_order carries him). Englert 2020 (read in full), conclusion: settler labour movements "fight simultaneously over the distribution of wealth generated through their labour and the distribution of the colonial loot accumulated through the dispossession of the indigenous population"; his cases are Palestine and South Africa, so the Canadian application is Burrill's. Re-proposes row 7 of the 2026-10-12 request, which is not on disk. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: Land as 'settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element': agriculture 'is inherently sedentary and, therefore, permanent' and 'progressively eats into Indigenous territory, a primitive accumulation that turns native flora and fauna into a dwindling resource' (Wolfe 2006); 'land is the irreducible element of settler colonialism' (Snelgrove et al. 2014)
edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), fourth section: "Of itself, however, modernity cannot explain the insatiable dynamic whereby settler colonialism always needs more land. The answer that springs most readily to mind is agriculture"; "Agriculture not only supports the other sectors. It is inherently sedentary and, therefore, permanent"; "The reproach of nomadism renders the native removable." Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, p. 30 (read): "land is the irreducible element of settler colonialism, and … environmental degradation has often proceeded through and in support of settler colonialism". Tuck and Yang 2012, p. 5 (read): "Within settler colonialism, the most important concern is land/water/air/subterranean earth". The dissertation evidence for the pairing is in the entry's scope_note, not here. Drawn by Agent B by the coordinator's decision; Agent C does not duplicate it. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

edges.relationship: The wilderness debate: Hays found 'a world of abstracted ideas … divorced from the values and ideas inherent in wilderness action' (1996, as quoted by Foreman); Sessions, habitat underweighted (1996); Foreman, that the 'Received Wilderness Idea' of 'Callicott, Cronon and other postmodern deconstructionist scholars' is 'a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground' (1998; 2000)
edges.evidence_note: Foreman 2000 read in full (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §2.2): pp. 32–33 and the reference list p. 38. Hays's sentence is carried only as quoted by Foreman (p. 32); Hays's comment (Environmental History 1:1, 29–32) is unread and the quotation is marked for re-verification. Sessions 1996 read in full (graph record). Callicott and Nelson 1998 known by publisher description and Foreman's own reference. Cronon's 1996 response (pp. 47–55) is unread: this edge records the critics' words; his 1995 defence of wild-land protection and nonhuman autonomy is on cronon_wilderness (reflow pp. 12, 17–20). Source strand environment/wilderness_debate.

edges.relationship: Wilderness as the erasure of Indigenous dwelling: 'The removal of Indians to create an "uninhabited wilderness"' shows 'just how invented, just how constructed, the American wilderness really is' (1995); the Apostle Islands, 'inhabited by Ojibwe peoples for centuries', 'a wilderness that has long been a place of human dwelling' (2003)
edges.evidence_note: Own words. 1995: author-hosted reflow p. 10 (graph record cronon_wilderness, read in full 2026-10-13). 2003: 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands', read in full in OCR (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §2.2, P6): the Ojibwe sentence on the scan's third page (Orion p. 38), 'a wilderness that has long been a place of human dwelling' and 'manage the Apostle Islands as a historical wilderness' (p. 39). Warren (1997) and Jacoby (2001), his doctoral students (CV p. 11), and Spence (1999, abstract read) wrote on the same removal; nothing read here connects their books to this essay, so they are named as context only. Target strand indigenous/land ('Land, identity and colonial change').

edges.relationship: History for land managers and the public: the Apostle Islands should be managed 'as a historical wilderness' whose policy 'should equally protect stories—stories of wild nature, stories of human history' (2003); as AHA president he asked historians to 'connect our professional stories with the concerns of the wider public' (2013)
edges.evidence_note: Own words. 2003 essay read in full in OCR (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §2.2): the riddle passage (p. 39) and the closing paragraph ('It is a storied wilderness'). 2013 address: open AHA text, passages (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §1.3). CV (read): Trust for Public Land board 2003–20; Wisconsin Historical Society curators 1997–2011; the 2012 column 'The Public Practice of History in and for a Digital Age' (title only). Target strand publichistory/place_preservation.

edges.relationship: 'The digital revolution has created endless opportunities via blogs, websites, YouTube, and social media' for the historian's stories (2013); presidential columns 'The Public Practice of History in and for a Digital Age' and 'Scholarly Authority in a Wikified World' (2012); 'digital scholarship' named among his fields
edges.evidence_note: Moderate. The 2013 sentence is read (open AHA text, data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §1.3); the 2012 Perspectives columns are known by title from the CV (p. 8) and his AHA-writings page; the CV (p. 1) lists 'digital scholarship' among his fields and (p. 10) the websites he built. The columns themselves are unread. No target strand: the entry's strands are per-work; the coordinator may attach it to the 2005 Cohen–Rosenzweig strand or leave it unattached.

edges.relationship: Leopold as teacher and model: the landscape-reading course he drew from Leopold (afterword, 2003), essays on Leopold and A Sand County Almanac (1998), and Leopold among the 'Classics and Precursors' of his reading list (2005)
edges.evidence_note: Afterword pp. 173–175 (graph record cronon_changes_afterword, read: the Wisconsin landscape training and Leopold's course model); CV p. 9 (read): 'A Voice in the Wilderness: Aldo Leopold' (Wilderness, 1998) and 'A Sand County Almanac' in A Wisconsin Fifteen (1998), titles only; the 2005 reading list (graph record pe131_carson_cronon_readings_2005, read). Parallels edge_911 (leopold → environment), which already cites the afterword.

edges.relationship: 'Modes of Prophecy and Production' answered Worster's 1990 agroecological programme (unread; reported by Isenberg 2013); 'A Place for Stories' (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy', set against Bonnifield's progressive plot
edges.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories' pp. 1347–1349 and 1363–1364 read (graph record pe131_cronon_place_stories_1992): the 'chief agent' and 'apocalyptic prophecy' sentences are at p. 1363, Worster's few pages on Indians at p. 1364. The 1990 response (JAH 76:4, 1122–31) is unread (OUP 403) and is known through Isenberg 2013, pp. 88–89 (read, graph record pe131_crosby_isenberg_2013); Cronon's CV p. 7 confirms the citation. A critique by reading, not a rejection: Cronon's essay treats both plots as narrative choices.
edges.map_label: Prophecy and production: reading Dust Bowl, 1990–92

edges.relationship: 'Gender and Environmental History' (1990) called his three levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and added 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction'
edges.evidence_note: Merchant's round-table response read in full (graph record pe131_merchant_jah_1990, pp. 1117–1121, author-hosted scan): the quoted phrases are already carried in donald_worster's description and scope note. Worster's essay is read in its 1993 reprint by search (graph record). Merchant's own entry is wave 2; this records Worster's reception.

edges.relationship: Agricultural capitalism as 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (Dust Bowl, 1979; 'The Dirty Thirties', 1986) and the West as 'a modern hydraulic society' (Rivers of Empire, 1985): the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level of environmental history (1990)
edges.evidence_note: No new reading: the quotations stand as recorded in the graph's existing records (Dust Bowl at the page given by Cronon 1992; Rivers of Empire via Hennessey 1987; 'The Dirty Thirties' read in full; the 1990 essay in the 1993 reprint by search) and in the entry's description. Proposed so that the capitalism entry names the environmental historian who made capitalism an ecological category; the coordinator chooses the strand (none of capitalismdebates' eleven strands names him; origin_of_capitalism or transition_debate are the nearest). data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md P6.

edges.relationship: A history of ecological ideas, Nature's Economy (1977; 2nd ed. 1994), and the essays 'History as Natural History' and 'The Ecology of Order and Chaos' (1993): a reviewer of his last book recalled 'his wonderful knack for synthesizing complex ideas' in Nature's Economy
edges.evidence_note: Nature's Economy: graph record (1977, snippets). The Wealth of Nature contents read on OUP (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §8: 'History as Natural History', 'The Ecology of Order and Chaos'). Collomb 2017 para. 5 read in full. The 1994 second edition is not verified here. Target strand science/ideas.

edges.relationship: Named objections across a career: McDean on generalising the Dust Bowl region (1986); Collomb on Shrinking the Earth, 'very short on details about the human capacity for adaptation', its 'plea for an earth ethic almost rings hollow' (2017), while calling him 'the greatest US environmental historian'
edges.evidence_note: McDean 1986 (graph record, read); Cronon's 1992 reading is carried by p4C_rel_11, not here; Collomb 2017 read in full (paras 3, 12–14) and Gratale 2017 read in full ('a critical and important contribution', para. 11) (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §8). Source strands environment/dust_causal_debate and environment/anthropocene_climate.

edges.relationship: 'Transformations of the Earth' opens on Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history' and his Kentucky canebrakes (1990/1993), as 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) had grounded the three levels in the same call
edges.evidence_note: The chapter's abstract on OUP, which is its opening paragraph, read (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §8); the 1988 appendix read in reprint (graph record pe131_worster_ends_1988). Parallels edge_911 (leopold → environment), which cites the same texts.

edges.relationship: Braudel, Febvre and Le Roy Ladurie named as French sources of ideas for environmental history in the 1990 essay and its 1993 reprint
edges.evidence_note: No new reading: the names are as recorded in the graph's records for the 1990 essay and the 1993 reprint (read by search, 2026-10-13) and used by edge_111 (annales → environment). A person-level re-sourcing of that edge.

edges.relationship: Conservation as dispossession: Indian removal made the 'uninhabited wilderness' of Yellowstone, Glacier and Yosemite (Spence 1999); the Stoney excluded from Banff for game, sport and assimilation (Binnema and Niemi 2006); northern game laws as state authority over hunting cultures (Sandlos 2007)
edges.evidence_note: Spence's OUP abstract read; the Binnema–Niemi and Piper–Sandlos abstracts read; Sandlos's UBC Press description read. Warren and Jacoby are not on this edge: their books are unread and no reader read here states a dispossession argument for them (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §§6–7). Source strand environment/conservation_dispossession; target strand indigenous/land. Overlaps edge_696 (indigenous ↔ environment, a comparison through Huggins, Bullard, Cronon and Carruthers), which stays.

edges.relationship: Canadian environmental histories of the fur-trade and northern worlds: the pemmican market that 'nearly wiped out the Canadian bison herds north of the Missouri River' (Colpitts 2014); ecological imperialism as 'a broken frontier' in the North (Piper and Sandlos 2007); Dene and Inuit hunters against conservationists (Sandlos 2007)
edges.evidence_note: Publisher descriptions and the 2007 abstract read; bodies unread (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §6.3). Reduced strength. Source strand environment/canadian_environmental_history; target strand native_newcomer/fur_trade_national_economy.

edges.relationship: Capital against the species: Malm's Fossil Capital (2016) holds that 'steam offered neither cheaper nor more abundant energy' but control over labour; Moore's Capitalism in the Web of Life (2015) and Stoll's 'A Metabolism of Society' (2014) ask what capitalism is for environmental historians; Worster had made agricultural capitalism 'the decisive factor' (1979)
edges.evidence_note: Malm's publisher page read; Moore metadata only; Stoll by chapter title in the Oxford Handbook contents; Worster's phrase as recorded in the graph's existing records (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §9). A teaching comparison, not a reception claim. Source strand environment/anthropocene_climate.

edge_892.relationship: Settler colonialism as 'a structure not an event': settler colonizers 'come to stay'; the form 'destroys to replace', is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal', has territory as its 'irreducible element' and persists after the frontier as 'structural genocide' (1994–2006)
edge_892.evidence_note: Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_01): the 2006 essay, read in full in the Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page (screq_wolfe_2006 addendum), joins the 1999 introduction (pp. 1–2, read earlier: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies'; 'invasion is a structure not an event'; contents and catalogue checked). Wolfe 2006, in his words: 'Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal' (p. 387, pages per Kauanui 2016); 'Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event' (p. 388; his note 7 refers the formula to the 1999 book, p. 2, and to 'Nation and MiscegeNation', 1994, p. 96); 'Settler colonialism destroys to replace'; 'elimination refers to more than the summary liquidation of Indigenous people, though it includes that' (p. 390); 'settler colonialism is relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' (p. 403). A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage (Veracini 2013; Kauanui 2016, note 7: Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973) precede it, and Kauanui records that Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did'. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note (user rule, 2026-10-23); bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

edge_893.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
edge_893.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_02): Veracini's obituary (read in full) reports that the 1999 book 'was ostensibly a history of Australian anthropology', that 'settler colonialism' was 'only added at the very end and at the request of the publisher', and that 'to explain the evolution of anthropology Patrick defined settler colonialism as distinct from colonialism'; Goeman (read in full) records Audra Simpson's memory of him as a historian 'of anthropology itself, and its relationship to politics'. The chapters remain unread, so the critique/contribution question stays open.

edge_882.relationship: Postcolonial studies 'failed to detect the settler colonial "situation" in its specific operation' (Veracini 2011); 'relying solely on postcolonial literatures … will not help to envision the shape that decolonization must take in settler colonial contexts' (Tuck and Yang 2012); postcolonial theory 'has tended to obscure the ongoing hierarchies of settler states' (Macoun and Strakosch 2013)

edge_881.relationship: Indigenous historical authority and settler-colonial analysis
edge_881.evidence_note: Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge settler colonial studies (abstract). Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_12) adds the read words on both sides. Kauanui 2016 (read in full): 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; Wolfe 'insisted … that Native scholars did' create the field; indigeneity 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'. Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, pp. 9–11 (read): the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study'. Goeman 2016 (read in full): Wolfe's work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies that at times leaves out Indigenous epistemologies and ontologies'. Veracini 2013 (author manuscript, read): 'indigenous studies, and especially history became crucial disciplinary sites in the development of "settler colonialism" as a conceptual category'. Comparison only: Indigenous history is not a subset of the paradigm, and the paradigm did not originate there. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note.

edge_883.evidence_note: Veracini dates a usage, until the late 1970s, naming a diehard hyper-colonialism challenged by anti-colonial insurgencies. Mamdani revisits the first postcolonial generation's political economy (Rodney) to ask how settler and native became political identities. Comparison: no line of descent from liberation politics to the later field is asserted. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_13): Veracini 2011, pp. 5–7 (read in full), 'Decolonisation is not settler decolonisation': 'arguing against colonialism is not the same thing as condemning settler colonialism'; 'if colonialism ends with the coloniser's departure … settler colonialism ends with an indigenous ultimate permanence'. Tuck and Yang 2012, p. 31 (read): 'Decolonization is not equivocal to other anti-colonial struggles. It is incommensurable.' Both keep the two decolonisations apart, which is why a comparison and not a descent is drawn.

edge_720.relationship: Environmental perspectives on city–hinterland connections, assessed in period by an urban historian as a contribution to urban history (1991–92); Castonguay and Evenden's Urban Rivers (2012) carry the city–river question across Europe and North America
edge_720.evidence_note: In-period evidence: the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (open PDF, text layer read). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context', and that Cronon 'has, perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward from its current relegation as a kind of assumed stage set for monographs on local occurrences in cities' (p. 491). Of the premise that 'to really understand how and why cities developed, one must study how they organized their hinterlands', he writes: 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates the explanatory power of this fundamental urban historical premise' (p. 492). He also finds that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon’s response: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change'; 'Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field, setting the process of urbanization in a broader context that is as important to urban historians as it is to environmental ones' (p. 520). The arrow rests on one book, one urban historian’s in-period assessment and the author’s reply; it does not claim that urban history as a field adopted environmental questions. Context only, not support for the claim: Cronon’s 1993 ASEH address names Joel Tarr’s 'many studies of pollution and waste streams' (p. 3, n. 6) and cites Melosi’s Garbage in the Cities (n. 24). cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. Cronon’s own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.131). Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_720 revision): the Pittsburgh page read (Mauch's blurb: 'the best environmental history of urban industrial rivers'); body unread.

edge_901.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995); and the field's institutions: ASEH president 1989–93, editor of the Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books 1994–2014 ('acquiring, editing, and writing forewords for all titles'), and in 2013 'the first self-described environmental historian ever to serve as president of the AHA'
edge_901.evidence_note: Cronon’s own in-period statements. Changes in the Land (1983), ch. 1 'The View from Walden', read in full in an unpaginated web transcription (page numbers not verified): 'The replacement of Indians by predominantly European populations in New England was as much an ecological as a cultural revolution'; 'An ecological history begins by assuming a dynamic and changing relationship between environment and culture, one as apt to produce contradictions as continuities. Moreover, it assumes that the interactions of the two are dialectical'; 'The choice is not between two landscapes, one with and one without a human influence; it is between two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'; 'The pig was not merely a pig but a creature bound among other things to the fence, the dandelion, and a very special definition of property'; a 'world capitalist system' draws people 'into trade and market relations which lie well beyond the boundaries of their local ecosystems'. He sets this against species-transfer accounts 'as Alfred Crosby and William H. McNeill have done', which are 'bound to be incomplete', and against functionalist ecological anthropology, which risks 'a static and ahistorical view'. In 1992 he calls Nature’s Metropolis 'a natural sequel' to that book, which 'described a comparable set of environmental changes that occurred in New England as that region became linked to London’s markets' (Annals of Iowa forum, p. 517). 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993): the lesson 'When people buy and sell things in a market, they link together ecosystems and encourage change' is 'a central concern of my own work' (p. 8, n. 14, citing Changes in the Land, Nature’s Metropolis and 'Kennecott Journey'); 'The chief moral of my own version of environmental history is the one I tried to embed in the title of my book Changes in the Land. To live as human beings on this planet is to change the world around us' (p. 19); 'the material history of environmental change is simultaneously a spiritual history of human consciousness and a political economic history of human society' (p. 19); 'All environmental knowledge is culturally constructed and historically contingent—including our own' (p. 14), held together with the claim that 'the natural world exists quite apart from what we believe about it' (p. 15). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 33): 'The special task of environmental historians is to tell stories that carry us back and forth across the boundary between people and nature to reveal just how culturally constructed that boundary is—and how dependent upon natural systems it remains.' 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995, author’s reflow p. 1): wilderness is 'quite profoundly a human creation'. A contribution, not a founding: he makes the claim for materialist analysis that tries 'to finesse a full-blown determinism' on behalf of the field ('One important contribution of environmental history', 1993, p. 13), and places the field among the 'new' histories of the 1960s (p. 2). Contested in period: Danbom (1992) reads Nature’s Metropolis for its 'environmental moralism' (p. 503) and as 'a book about evil unleavened by good' (p. 506); Cronon answers 'I see no pure heroes or pure villains in the stories I tell' (p. 522). His 1990 JAH response to Worster is unread. The 2003 afterword (pp. 182–185: property analysis learned from anthropology, economics and legal theory; his own criticism of schematic capitalism and source asymmetry) is a later reading. edge_342 (anthropology → environment) and edge_343 (environment → culture) stay: they record anthropology as a resource and environmental history’s contribution to cultural history; this arrow is his own framework. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_901 revision): CV pp. 2, 14–15 read in full; the AHA's open text of 'Storytelling' read in passages.

edge_903.relationship: Narrative bounded by evidence, ecology and the community of scholars: an environmental historian’s answer to postmodern critiques of narrative (1992); twenty years on, 'Storytelling' (2013) restated the case: 'How do we make the past come alive? By telling stories about it', referring readers to the 1992 essay for 'this theoretical background'
edge_903.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative', JAH 78:4 (March 1992), author-hosted copy in journal pagination (pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read). Writing about narrative, 'we cannot avoid encountering the postmodernist assault on narrative, which calls into question not just the stories we tell but the deeper purpose that motivated us in the first place' (p. 1349). The argument is meant for all historians: 'I am urging historians to acknowledge storytelling as the necessary core even of longue durée histories … Environmental history is but one example of these, and most of my arguments apply just as readily to the others' (p. 1349, n. 5). 'I, like most practicing historians, am only willing to follow the postmodernists so far'; 'My goal throughout has been to acknowledge the immense power of narrative while still defending the past (and nature) as real things to which our storytelling must somehow conform lest it cease being history altogether' (p. 1372). Three bounds: 'our stories cannot contravene known facts about the past' and 'our stories must make ecological sense' (p. 1372); 'We write as members of communities' (p. 1373). 'To just that extent, nature coauthors our stories' (p. 1373). Against 'an endless postmodernist deconstruction of texts that fails to ground itself in history, in community, in politics, and finally in the moral problem of living on earth' he asserts 'the virtues of narrative' (p. 1374), and he asks environmental historians for 'not just stories about nature, but stories about stories about nature' (p. 1375). He reads with Hayden White’s Metahistory, Tropics of Discourse and The Content of the Form and with Novick (nn. 6, 7, 43), and credits Richard White with the argument about criticism (n. 46). The 1993 address restates it: historical wisdom 'usually comes in the form of parables, not policy recommendations or certainties' (p. 16). This is his own text; no in-period reading that places the essay in the postmodernism debate was read. edge_904.relationship: Three levels of environmental history (nature, modes of production, ideas), with the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level (1979–1990); and, at the end, the 'Second Earth' of 1500 whose abundance gave 'the false impression that there was no limit' (Shrinking the Earth, 2016, as read by Collomb)
edge_904.evidence_note: Worster's own statements, in-period first. 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth (1988), read in an abridged reprint and checked by full-text search of the 1988 edition, whose running heads place the passage between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013 cites p. 293): 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues it addresses'; 'The first deals with understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in past times'; 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment. Here we are concerned with tools and work, with the social relations that grow out of that work, with the various modes people have devised of producing goods from natural resources'; the third is 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics, laws, myths, and other structures of meaning become part of an individual's or group's dialogue with nature'; together they 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990; English text checked in Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature, ch. 4; JAH page as cited by Isenberg): 'most environmental historians seem to have settled philosophically on a position that is at once materialist and idealist', yet the essay turns to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena' (p. 1091), and proposes that 'the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation”'. Dust Bowl (1979) had argued: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (p. 5, as quoted by Cronon 1992, p. 1363; wording confirmed in the 1979 edition). In-period readings: Merchant's 1990 response (read) calls his 'conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition' 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field', while the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117). Cronon (1992, read) finds that in Dust Bowl 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism', a plot that 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy' (p. 1363). McDean (1986) criticises the generalisation across the Plains (existing source, not re-read). A contribution, not a founding: Worster takes the idea from Aldo Leopold, who 'spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history”' (1988), and McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013, pp. 88–89) reports White's and Cronon's 1990 objections ('superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense'; 'potentially excessive materialism'), whose texts are unread here; McNeill (2003, p. 37) writes of environmental historians' theories that 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', but that such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm'. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_904 revision): Collomb 2017 para. 2 read in full; Shrinking the Earth itself unread; the Origins page (Hall chair from 1989 until retirement) and the AHA award list (2012) read.

Every edge rests on a read text in the author's own words or on a named reader's explicit statement, and the notes say which: Stoler's 2002 abstract; Along the Archival Grain through Gouda and Schulte Nordholt (read in full, page numbers given); Carnal Knowledge through Ottevaere; Imperial Debris through Schultz; Trouillot through Craipain (p. 98), Bulamah–Goyatá–Pereira and Davidson (unpaginated; wording awaits a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1); Cook 2001 in part; Schwartz–Cook, Mbembe, Manoff, Zeitlyn by abstract. Research of 2026-10-23: data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md (Agent B: readings §§1–16; proposals P.1–P.12). Every edge rests on a read text in the author's own words or on a named reader's explicit statement, and the notes say which; publisher descriptions and Crossref records are marked as such. Wolfe 2006 was read in an Internet Archive capture of the journal's own free-to-read page (coordinator decision c, 2026-10-23); Veracini 2011 and 2013 and Macoun and Strakosch 2013 in the authors' institutional deposits. The dissertation figures (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23) sit in the scope note, coverage basis and strand text only; the Canadian PhD counts formerly in the notes of edge_892, edge_881 and edge_882 are struck (user rule). Coordinator decisions of 2026-10-23: period_4 stays as set by 1.155; Veracini, Simpson and Coulthard get roster rows and QIDs, entries in wave 2 (p4B_rel_06 held); p4B_rel_16 drawn here and not by Agent C; the Black-studies edge held. Every new edge rests on a text read in the author's own words (Foreman 2000, Cronon 2003 and 2013, Collomb and Gratale 2017) or on named readers already read in the graph (Merchant 1990, Cronon 1992, McDean 1986, Sessions 1996); abstract-only, description-only and 'as quoted by' evidence is labelled in each note, and no edge rests on the dissertation data, which appear only in scope_note, strand focus and coverage, with the founder selection, lift threshold and sampling stated and interpreted as an associated readership pattern, not as decline. Unread texts (the 1996 comments and response, Sutter 2013, McNeill 2000/2003, the 2005 forum, the Canadian books' bodies) are named in the scope notes. text_revisions.old: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
text_revisions.new: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, took land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe gave the field its programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'invasion is a structure not an event' (1999, 2006). Lorenzo Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011) and distinguished colonialism ('you, work for me') from settler colonialism ('you, go away'), adding that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': it 'extinguishes itself'. Two questions organise this selection: how elimination persists while pursuing its own completion, and how settler-colonial analysis relates to Indigenous sovereignty, refusal and resurgence. Veracini develops Wolfe's formula: self-supersession means the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, not a successful decolonisation. The Indigenous reading adopts Wolfe's formula while insisting that 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies' (Kauanui), that 'decolonization is not a metaphor' (Tuck and Yang) and that refusal, not recognition, answers the settler state (Simpson, Coulthard). Settler scholars warn against 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch); Marxists ask whether elimination or exploitation defines the form (Englert). In Canada the frame met an older historiography of reserves, treaties, gender and the state, and the TRC's finding of 'cultural genocide' (2015).

text_revisions.old: A selective research field whose theoretical consolidation came mostly after 2000; the entry covers its roots through 2000 and cites selected later works as readings. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies. Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris and Daschuk wrote earlier or beside it. No single founder, origin or Canadian consensus is asserted. Critics appear as critics. Francophone uptake in the PhD corpus is near zero.

B. Simpson; Rowse; Konishi; Sexton; Garba and Sorentino; King; Daschuk; Miller 2009; Perry 2015; Carter 2016; McCallum; Mawani; Stanger-Ross; Lowman and Barker; Regan. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies; Veracini (2013) and Kauanui (2016) both record uses of the term before Wolfe (Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973, Denoon 1983, Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis 1995). Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris, Miller, Daschuk and McCallum wrote earlier or beside it, and their publisher descriptions do not use the phrase. Critics appear as critics; Kauanui and Goeman defend Wolfe's theory against shallow citation while asking the field to attend to Indigenous studies. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: two or more of the field's authors are cited by 3.2% of Canada + US theses in 2000–09 and 11.0% in 2020–25 (Canada 15.2%, US 6.8%); Wolfe and Veracini are co-cited by 3.0% of theses in 2020–25 and Wolfe with Tuck and Yang, Simpson or Coulthard by 2.3% (the release's category 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' names a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position: Tuck and Yang build on Wolfe, and Kauanui criticises his reception), the only rising two-sided citing after 2000; the Canadian neighbourhood of the founders is the largest and youngest of any field (51 works, median year 2006), its 2020–25 entrants Coulthard, Simpson, Carter, Miller, Daschuk, Kauanui and Greer. The earlier pilot of 2026-10-12 (Canadian strict History PhDs, 2009–26) found 54 citing a work of Wolfe's and 17 the 1999 book (first in 2012), and Daschuk the work most co-cited with Wolfe and Veracini (19 of 58); these figures say more about Canadian history than about him. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Francophone uptake in the corpus remains near zero.
